sections.html:
The topic of leeches in shrimp tanks is controversial because opinions vary on whether they pose a threat to shrimp. The main issue is that aquarists often cannot identify the leech species in their tanks. The Asian leech (Barbronia weberi) is one of the most common leeches in the world and is a predatory leech, making it an extremely unwelcome guest in a shrimp tank.

Taxonomy

DomainEukaryota (organisms with cells)
KingdomAnimalia (animals)
PhylumAnnelida (segmented worms)
ClassClitellata (clitellates)
SubclassHirudinea (leeches)
OrderArhynchobdellida (jawless leeches)
FamilySalifidae (freshwater predacious leeches)
GenusBarbronia
SpeciesB. weberi

The genus currently contains eight species: B. arcana, B. assiuti, B. borealis, B. gwalagwalensis, B. nepalensis, B. rouxi, B. shillongensis and B. weberi.

Note: the genus Barbronia draws significant scientific interest due to its rapid global expansion facilitated by human introductions. The capability of a single leech to produce hundreds of offspring annually, even without mating, is a key factor.

Description

  • Size. Small leeches, generally up to 2.5–3.5 cm (1.0–1.4 in) long with a maximum body width of 3.3 mm (0.13 in). They can stretch their bodies to 2–3 times their original length.
  • Shape. The body is elongated, segmented, worm-like and tapers towards the front. Tiny bumps cover the body, giving it a rough texture.
  • Suckers. The anterior sucker has a maximum width of 0.9 mm (0.035 in); the posterior sucker has a maximum width of 2.0 mm (0.079 in) and is directed ventrally.
  • Colour. Usually reddish to brownish-yellow, with a whitish ventral side. Pigmentation is minimal.
  • Eyes. 3 pairs of circular eyespots.
  • Reproductive organs. The gonopores are large, clearly visible and separated by 5.5 annuli.

For a detailed description of Barbronia weberi, see the scientific papers listed in the references.

Lifespan

According to the study, the average lifespan of Barbronia weberi is about 122 days. The maximum recorded was 216 days, which can be considered an exception rather than the norm.

Are Asian leeches dangerous to shrimp, fish and snails?

Shrimp tanks. No, by no means is it safe to have Asian leeches in shrimp tanks. These leeches are fast enough to catch not only weak but also healthy shrimp. Molting shrimp are an easy meal for them.

Some aquarists online claim they have never had issues with leeches in their shrimp tanks. The author believes they may be mistaken, mainly about the type of leech, because not all leech species pose a threat to shrimp. Since identifying leech species requires specialized equipment, it is better to err on the side of caution: if you spot leeches in your aquarium, assume the worst and try to remove them immediately.

Snail tanks. Freshwater snails are not the primary food source for this leech, but there have been cases of hungry leeches attacking snails. Be cautious, especially with decorative snail species that do not have an operculum (trapdoor) allowing them to close their shell when threatened.

Fish tanks. Asian leeches cannot harm fish. On the contrary, many fish species will eat them; the leech's movements trigger their hunting instinct.

Originally, Barbronia weberi had a native range from Afghanistan and Pakistan to Java, Sumatra, Borneo, India and Southern China.

In recent years the Asian leech has established populations on every continent except Antarctica. It was introduced to South and North America, Australia, New Zealand and Europe (Italy, England, Hungary, Austria and Germany).

The aquarium trade is the most probable source of introduction of this species.

These leeches generally prefer stagnant water (ponds, lakes, swamps, etc.) or slow-moving bodies of water. They are often associated with aquatic vegetation, using plants for the attachment of cocoons.

How do Asian leeches get into our tanks?

It is very easy to accidentally introduce Asian leeches. They are often associated with aquatic vegetation (such as the waterweeds Hydrilla verticillata, Elodea sp., etc.), so their eggs often hitchhike on aquatic plants. In most cases they are too small to see, and a few weeks later you start to see them in the tank. Sometimes they also arrive with new live food, particularly worms.

How to get rid of Asian leeches

Unless it is a bare-bottom tank, it is almost impossible to get rid of them. The author checked many forums, asked other aquarists and tried several methods personally, such as salt, dog dewormer and anti-planaria products, but none seemed to work. Very high concentrations of these products might be effective, but that was not feasible because they could also harm the shrimp. Elevated concentrations of copper are not an option either.

One study reported that Barbronia weberi does not like warm water (above 30 °C / 86 °F); the author has not yet had the opportunity to test this.

Copper

Copper is very dangerous in fish and shrimp keeping. All crustaceans, such as dwarf shrimp, crabs and crayfish, are especially sensitive to it.

  • Buy a copper test kit.
  • Lower the water volume as much as you can. The more water you drain, the more effective the treatment can be.
  • Add copper sulfate. The concentration should be at least 1.5–2 mg/l (the source also states “5 – 2 ppm”, an apparent typo; 1 mg/l equals 1 ppm).
  • Leave the tank for 3 days.
  • Fill the tank and do a large water change.
  • Fill the tank again and test the copper level.
  • Remove the copper before adding fish or shrimp back.

Downside: any residual traces of copper can still kill dwarf shrimp when you move them back.

The nuclear option

  • Move all shrimp and snails into another bare-bottom (quarantine) tank.
  • Visually check that no leeches were transferred.
  • Tear the tank down completely.
  • Scrub and clean the tanks, decorations and driftwood with hydrogen peroxide.
  • Leave them in the sun to dry for a few days.
  • Throw away the sponge (replace the filter media).
  • Quarantine plants.
  • Ideally, never re-use substrate from an infested tank. If you still want to, boil it or pour boiling water from a kettle onto it, stirring to kill everything in it. To be sure, add bleach for 5–10 minutes.

Introducing leech-eating fish

Many fish eat leeches. Cichlids (such as Julidochromis, Oscar, Red Devils), loaches (such as clown loaches, Zebra Botia and Macracantha Botia, the latter being the same species as the clown loach), bettas, mollies, tetras, pea puffers, etc. will often go straight after them.

Downsides:

  • You have to add a new fish you may not want. Even a small fish such as cardinal tetras or guppies is not safe for shrimp tanks.
  • In large tanks, once leeches are established, even fish might not wipe them out completely, or it will take a long time. They hide in the substrate and are not seen in the daytime, but they are there.

Manual removal trap

Use tweezers to grasp the leech by its body. (The source gives no further instructions.)

How to prevent infestation

The best way to keep Asian leeches (and any pests or parasites) out of your tanks is to head off the problem before it takes hold. Always quarantine everything, and treat everything as if it were heavily infected: plants, rocks, driftwood, decorations, etc. – anything from another source that may have been in contact with biological material. With an extended quarantine you will notice any leeches and can deal with them.

All leeches of the family Salifidae and genus Barbronia are freshwater predacious leeches. According to the study, in the wild Barbronia weberi feeds on a range of invertebrates including oligochaetes (worms), snails, crustaceans and even insects.

In aquariums their main food is all kinds of worms, including:

  • Tubifex worms
  • Bloodworms
  • Blackworms
  • Detritus worms
  • Grindal worms

Although adult leeches can go for long periods without food, once they gain access to food their appetite becomes insatiable. Cannibalism among them is also not uncommon.

Do Asian leeches eat planaria?

Some aquarists have reported that after these leeches appeared, the number of planaria in their tanks dropped sharply. This suggests planaria could theoretically be part of the leeches' diet, but this is currently speculation and requires more evidence.

Asian leeches typically inhabit substrates where they have access to decomposing organic matter or small organisms, such as worms, which they feed on.

They can swim using undulating movements through water, but this is not their primary mode of transportation.

They are nocturnal. However, their activity patterns can also be influenced by food availability, environmental conditions and the presence of predators.

Although leeches may congregate in areas with high food availability or during mating, they are not considered social animals. They lead solitary lives.

Life cycle

  • Egg: adults lay eggs in a gelatinous cocoon deposited on plants.
  • Embryo: the eggs hatch into embryos within the cocoon, which develop and grow inside until ready to hatch.
  • Juvenile: after hatching, the young leeches emerge from the cocoon as tiny copies of the adults.
  • Growth and development: juveniles prey and feed on organic matter, growing over time. As they feed, they undergo several molts, shedding their outer layer to accommodate their increasing size.
  • Maturity: the leeches reach sexual maturity and become adults, which reproduce and produce eggs, continuing the cycle.

Reproduction

Barbronia weberi is a hermaphrodite species: each individual has both male and female reproductive organs and assumes both roles simultaneously during mating.

However, the study also found that Asian leeches can reproduce without cross-fertilization. Therefore, it takes only one leech in the aquarium for an infestation to occur later on.

  • Produces cocoons every week for up to three months, at which time the adults begin to senesce.
  • Cocoons are attached to aquatic vegetation, rocks or the sides of aquariums. On leaves they are usually attached near the base of leaf whorls or along the stem, making them difficult to see.
  • Cocoons generally contain 1 to 5 eggs.
  • Eggs hatch within the cocoon after 2 days, and larvae/juveniles remain within the cocoon for 25–30 days.
  • The fluid inside the cocoons contains all the nutrients required for growth and development, as the parent provides no food or care after cocoon production.
  • After leaving the cocoon, the young leeches are 5–6 mm (0.2 in) long.
  • Emerging young can feed on prey larger than themselves. Most survive to maturity after their first meal, but if they do not feed within a day, they usually die.
  • Parents did not interact with cocoons or young after hatching, except for cannibalism when adults ate the young.
  • Depending on temperature and food availability, they become adults and reach reproductive maturity within 2–4 months.

The Asian leech (Barbronia weberi) is typically a freshwater predator of invertebrates. In aquariums they usually arrive on plants, and even one individual is enough for an infestation within months.

It is really hard to get rid of them because this invasive leech is highly resilient, and practically anything that can kill it will also harm your shrimp. That is why the primary method of combating them is prevention: avoid adding untreated or unquarantined plants to your aquarium.
